explanations.explanation: That's the plan, friend. Sarai, Abram's wife, says, "Please go to my maidservant; perhaps I can build a family by her." Hagar is her Egyptian maidservant. And the verse ends with Abram listening to the voice of Sarai.

explanations.answer: Make his servant Eliezer his heir
explanations.explanation: Good memory, because Eliezer of Damascus does come up. Abram mentioned him as the heir of his house back in Genesis 15:2. But that's not Sarai's plan here. In Genesis 16:2 she asks Abram to go to her maidservant Hagar.

explanations.answer: Move the household back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt does connect to this story, since Hagar is Egyptian. But nobody in this passage packs a single bag for it. Sarai's plan stays right at home. She asks Abram, her husband, to go to her maidservant Hagar.

Ten it is. The text says this happens "…after he had lived in Canaan for ten years…" Canaan is the land where Abram and Sarai are living. Then Sarai takes her maidservant Hagar and gives her to Abram to be his wife.

Seven, friend? That's a fine number. It's just not the one in the verse. Genesis 16:3 says Abram had lived in Canaan for ten years when Sarai gave her maidservant Hagar to him. Ten years of living in the land, and Sarai still has no child. That's a long stretch of waiting.

Forty is a big number, friend. The Bible uses it in other places, like the rain in Genesis 7:12. But this verse is smaller than that. Genesis 16:3 says Abram had lived in Canaan for ten years when Sarai gave Hagar to him. Ten, not forty.
Yes. The text says Hagar "…began to despise her mistress." Her mistress is Sarai, the woman who owns her household service. Sarai later says Hagar has treated her with contempt (Genesis 16:5).

Envy sounds believable, but it isn't the word the text uses. Genesis 16:4 says Hagar "…began to despise her mistress." Despise is a stronger word than envy. Sarai's own words later back it up when she says Hagar has treated her with contempt (Genesis 16:5).

Pity would have made for a much quieter story, friend. The text goes the other way. Hagar, Sarai's maidservant, "…began to despise her mistress." Sarai then says Hagar has treated her with contempt (Genesis 16:5).
True. Sarai says, "May the LORD judge between you and me." She says it to Abram, her husband. She also says she delivered her servant into his arms.

Not false, friend, because she really does say it. Genesis 16:5 has Sarai telling Abram, "May the LORD judge between you and me." Sarai is Abram's wife. She's speaking to her husband when she says it.

That's what he says. Abram tells Sarai, "your servant is in your hands. Do whatever you want with her." Then Sarai treats Hagar so harshly that Hagar flees. Heavy moment, and I think it's a hard one to read.

The text goes the other direction, friend. Abram says, "your servant is in your hands. Do whatever you want with her." That puts Hagar in Sarai's hands, not his. I think this is one of the heavier lines in the passage.

explanations.answer: She should go back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Nobody in the passage says that to Hagar. Abram answers Sarai with, "your servant is in your hands. Do whatever you want with her." Sarai then treats Hagar so harshly that she flees. It's a heavy part of the story.
Yes. Sarai treats Hagar so harshly "…that she fled from her." Hagar, the maidservant, takes off. By the next verse she's out in the desert.
The text never shows Hagar asking Abram for anything. Genesis 16:6 says Sarai treated her so harshly that she fled from her. Hagar runs. Then verse 7 finds her out in the desert.

Hiding in Abram's tent isn't what the text says, friend. Genesis 16:6 says Sarai treated Hagar so harshly that “…she fled from her.” I think this part hurts, because Hagar was treated so badly that she ran. Then verse 7 says the angel of the LORD found her by a spring in the desert.

explanations.answer: Go back and submit to Sarai
explanations.explanation: That's the instruction. The angel of the LORD tells her, "Return to your mistress and submit to her authority." Hagar has just said she's running away from Sarai, so this is a big ask. The text doesn't say how she feels about it, so I'll only guess: I think that was a lot to hear.

Keep going and never return? The angel says the opposite. He tells Hagar, "Return to your mistress and submit to her authority." Hagar had just said she was running away from Sarai. I bet she didn't expect to hear that one.

explanations.answer: Wait at the spring for Abram
explanations.explanation: The spring is where the angel finds her, friend, so that part is true. But nobody tells her to wait for Abram. The angel says, "Return to your mistress and submit to her authority." Sarai is the mistress he means.

True. The angel says, "I will greatly multiply your offspring so that they will be too numerous to count." That's a big promise for a woman who has just been found by a spring in the desert. And it comes from the angel of the LORD himself.

Not false, friend. Genesis 16:10 has the angel adding, "I will greatly multiply your offspring so that they will be too numerous to count." The promise is made right there at the spring. It's made to Hagar.

explanations.answer: The LORD has heard her cry
explanations.explanation: Yes. The angel says to name him Ishmael, "…for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction." The reason is that the LORD heard her. That's the whole reason the angel gives.

explanations.answer: The LORD will make him a king
explanations.explanation: A king would be a big reason for a name, but the angel doesn't say it. He gives a different one: "…for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction." No throne is mentioned in this passage. The name goes with her cry being heard.

explanations.answer: He'll be born beside a spring
explanations.explanation: The spring matters in this story, but the angel doesn't tie it to the name. He says the boy's name is Ishmael "…for the LORD has heard your cry of affliction." The reason is her cry. Nothing in the passage says where the boy will be born.

The angel says the opposite, friend. He says, "he will live in hostility toward all his brothers." He also says Ishmael's hand will be against everyone and everyone's hand against him. Peace isn't in that description.

False is right. The angel says Ishmael will be "…a wild donkey of a man…" and that "he will live in hostility toward all his brothers." That's the opposite of living in peace. I think this is a heavy part of the passage, and the text doesn't soften it.

Yes. Hagar says, "You are the God who sees me…" and she gives that name to the LORD who spoke to her. She's a servant who ran into the desert, and she says He sees her. I know a little about feeling unseen, and I think that name hits hard.

That's a lovely name for God, but it isn't the one Hagar gives. In Genesis 16:13 she says, "You are the God who sees me…" She's talking about the LORD who had just spoken to her at the spring. Her name for Him is about being seen.

That name does show up later in Moses' story, where God is called the God of the fathers (Exodus 3:15). But it isn't the name Hagar gives. In Genesis 16:13 she says, “You are the God who sees me…” about the LORD who spoke to her at the spring. Her name for Him is all about being seen.
Abram it is. The text says, "…Abram gave the name Ishmael to the son she had borne." Hagar is the mother, but Abram does the naming. Notice that it's the very name the angel gave in verse 11.

Hagar is the one who bears the son, friend, but she isn't the one who names him in verse 15. The text says, "…Abram gave the name Ishmael to the son she had borne." Hagar heard the name from the angel in verse 11. Abram is the one who gives it.

Sarai is Abram's wife, and she's all over this chapter. But verse 15 gives the naming to someone else. It says, "…Abram gave the name Ishmael to the son she had borne." The text doesn't say Sarai names the boy.

Eighty-six is it, and you've got Abram's age on the dot. Genesis 16:16 says, “Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to him.” I can't even remember what I did last year, and you're out here with exact ages. I'm proud of you, baker.
Seventy-five is a real number in Abram's story. He was seventy-five when he left Haran (Genesis 12:4). But by the time Ishmael is born, he's older. Genesis 16:16 says he was eighty-six.

Ninety-nine, friend? You jumped ahead like someone sneaking a taste of the dough before the batch is even mixed! That number does belong to Abram later, in Genesis 17:1. But Genesis 16:16 says, “Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to him.” Keep that ninety-nine in your apron pocket, because it's coming.
